title: Why nanomaterials behave differently

levels.label: Nanoparticle
levels.ask: Why does surface area matter at the nano scale?

explain.say: A nanometre is a billionth of a metre. A nanomaterial has pieces between 1 and 100 nanometres across, so small that about a thousand would fit across a single human hair.

levels.label: Nanoparticle
levels.ask: Why does surface area matter at the nano scale?

explain.say: Zoom in from a hair to a blood cell to a bacterium, and you are still far bigger than the nano scale. A nanoparticle may be only a few hundred or thousand atoms across.

levels.label: Nanoparticle
levels.ask: Why does surface area matter at the nano scale?

explain.say: At this size, a big share of the atoms sit on the surface, and that changes how a material behaves. Gold nanoparticles look red or purple, not gold, and they can speed up chemical reactions that a lump of gold cannot.

levels.label: Nanoparticle
levels.ask: Why does surface area matter at the nano scale?

explain.say: Engineers use these effects on purpose. Zinc oxide nanoparticles in sunscreen block ultraviolet light yet look clear, and graphene, a sheet of carbon just one atom thick, is incredibly strong for its weight.

levels.label: Nanoparticle
levels.ask: Why does surface area matter at the nano scale?

faq.a: A nanometre is one billionth of a metre, or a millionth of a millimetre. A human hair is about 80,000 nanometres wide, and a few atoms side by side make about one nanometre.
A nanoparticle is a particle between 1 and 100 nanometres across. It is big enough to contain hundreds to millions of atoms but small enough that its surface atoms strongly affect its properties.

faq.q: Why does surface area matter at the nano scale?
faq.a: Chop a material into tinier pieces and more of its atoms end up on the surface, where they can react and interact with light. That is why nanoparticles can be more reactive or a different colour from the same material in bulk.

In tiny gold particles, the electrons on the surface vibrate together and absorb green light, so the light left over looks red or purple. Medieval glassmakers used this, without knowing why, to colour stained glass.
asks: Why does nano gold change colour?

faq.a: Graphene is a single layer of carbon atoms joined in a honeycomb pattern. It is extremely strong for its weight, conducts electricity and heat very well, and is almost transparent.

facts: One nanometre is one billionth of a metre.
Graphene was first isolated in 2004 by Andre Geim and Konstantin Novoselov, who won the 2010 Nobel Prize in Physics.
The Roman Lycurgus Cup contains gold and silver nanoparticles that make it look green in reflected light and red when lit from behind.

quiz.say: Why can a material behave differently as nanoparticles?

options.show: A large share of their atoms are on the surface
options.say: A large share of their atoms are on the surface

options.show: They are made of different atoms
options.say: They are made of different atoms

quiz.why: With so many atoms at the surface, effects like reactivity and colour change.

wrong.1: The atoms are the same; only the size of the pieces changes.
wrong.2: Temperature is not the reason; surface area and size are.
